strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in LLM agent systems: scalable, history-aware tool and agent routing in large, dynamic environments (e.g., Model Context Protocol ecosystems) where static prompting and flat embedding retrieval struggle.

Well-designed data synthesis and training framework that couples graph-based evolutionary candidate mutation (to generate fine-grained hard negatives and functionally related tools) with multi-agent multi-turn trajectory simulation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across established benchmarks (MCP-Universe and MCP-Mark) against a wide variety of baselines, including embedding retrievers, ReAct agents, and leading generalist LLMs.
Thorough analysis of robustness and scalability against noisy distractors (+LiveMCP, +Mutation) and candidate space scaling, accompanied by reporting standard deviations across multiple runs.

Informative ablation studies highlighting the distinct benefits of history-aware conditioning and candidate mutation, supported by human verification of simulated trajectory quality (Cohen's Kappa = 0.93) and compelling zero-shot transfer to agent routing.
weaknesses: The operational details of how the candidate set C is presented to the 8B router at inference time under massive candidate spaces need clearer specification (e.g., whether all candidates are passed in-context simultaneously, filtered via a coarse retrieval stage, or ranked iteratively).
The Agent Route Benchmark relies on a relatively modest test set (156 samples) generated through a similar synthetic multi-agent simulation pipeline, which may inherit synthetic distribution biases.

The evaluation primarily measures routing accuracy at decision points; providing end-to-end task success rates / pass rates when downstream execution is completed would further substantiate the real-world operational impact of the router.

strengths: Addresses an important and highly timely problem: dynamic, history-aware tool and agent routing in large-scale, open environments (e.g., Model Context Protocol / MCP ecosystem and multi-agent systems).

The methodological pipeline is well-conceived, combining candidate graph construction, mutation operators that inject realistic functional hard negatives, and multi-agent simulation to produce supervision signals conditioned on execution history.

Empirical evaluation is extensive, spanning established benchmarks (MCP-Universe, MCP-Mark) across multiple domains, testing scalability/robustness against distractor tools, and comparing against competitive closed-source LLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude) and embedding baselines.

Ablation studies clearly demonstrate the isolated utility of incorporating dialogue history and self-evolutionary mutation, supported by human verification of simulated data reliability (Cohen's Kappa = 0.93) and reporting of variance across 5 runs.
weaknesses: The mechanism by which the 8B parameterized router handles large candidate spaces C at inference time is underspecified in Section 3: it is unclear whether all candidates in C are populated directly into the router's context window or if a coarse-to-fine filtering step precedes scoring, which is critical when scaling to thousands of tools/agents.

Baselines in Table 1 use generalist foundation models primarily via prompting/in-context routing, whereas ACE-Router is fine-tuned via LoRA on 15k task-specific synthetic trajectories; additional details on the exact prompt format and candidate budgeting for LLM baselines would strengthen fairness analysis.

The Agent Route Benchmark evaluation is relatively small (156 samples) and relies on the same synthetic generation scheme as the pipeline, meaning evaluation reflects simulated matching accuracy rather than end-to-end task completion in real multi-agent execution environments.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in agentic AI: moving beyond static tool injection and single-turn semantic retrieval towards context- and history-aware dynamic routing within expanding tool ecosystems like MCP.

Well-designed data synthesis methodology that pairs candidate graph construction and self-evolutionary mutation with random-walk trajectory simulation, effectively synthesizing realistic multi-turn interaction histories and hard-negative distractors without requiring live API infrastructure.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning standard benchmarks (MCP-Universe, MCP-Mark) against a wide variety of baselines, including embedding retrievers, ReAct architectures, and proprietary frontier models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Sonnet-4).

Thorough ablation and robustness analysis, including verification of the necessity of history, mutation data augmentation, and resistance to noisy/expanded candidate sets, accompanied by multi-run variance reporting and human verification (Cohen's Kappa = 0.93) of simulated trajectories.
weaknesses: Inference-time scalability bottleneck is not fully resolved: while the method addresses multi-turn routing over hundreds of tools, the paper is somewhat vague regarding how massive candidate spaces (e.g., thousands to millions envisioned in the 'Agent Web') are ingested by the router's context window during inference without hitting context limits or requiring an initial retrieval stage.

The Agent Routing evaluation relies entirely on an in-house synthetic benchmark of only 156 samples constructed using the same mutation/simulation paradigm as the training data, raising potential concerns regarding shared synthetic distribution bias.

The environment-free simulation relies entirely on LLM-generated execution outputs; without execution on real APIs during trajectory creation, simulated error dynamics may diverge from real-world API failures and edge cases.
Incomplete paper presentation: The repository URL is left blank in the abstract ('Our code is available at').

strengths: Timely and well-motivated focus on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem, addressing the core limitations of static injection and embedding-based retrieval in dynamic, multi-turn agent environments.
Well-designed data synthesis methodology that couples graph-based candidate structuring with self-evolutionary mutation operators to introduce fine-grained functional variants and hard negatives.

Strong empirical results: fine-tuning an open 8B model (Qwen3-8B) with the synthesized history-aware data enables it to outperform frontier proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Sonnet-4) across MCP-Universe and MCP-Mark.
Comprehensive robustness experiments demonstrating strong resilience against distractor tools and scale degradation, along with intriguing zero-shot generalization to agent routing.
Thorough appendix documentation providing detailed schemas, mutation operator definitions, and concrete prompt templates.
weaknesses: Unclear explanation of candidate space handling at inference time: Eq. (2) and Section 3.2 formulate selection over candidate set C, but it is not explicitly clarified how massive candidate sets (e.g., thousands of tools across servers) are passed to the 8B router without exceeding context limits or introducing latency bottlenecks (i.e., whether candidates are ranked individually, batched, or pre-filtered).

Ambiguity in metric definitions: Table 1 reports 'Accuracy (%)', but given that Gemini-2.5-Pro is fixed as the downstream reasoning model, it is ambiguous whether this reflects routing accuracy (matching ground-truth tool choice per turn) or downstream end-to-end task success rate.

The Agent Route benchmark is relatively limited in scale (156 synthetic test cases constructed by the authors), and Figure 3 (radar chart) lacks a corresponding table reporting exact baseline numbers.

Lack of quality control or human validation on LLM-simulated trajectories: Because training data is generated via an environment-free multi-agent simulation without real API execution, potential hallucinated parameters or unrealistic state transitions could affect the router, but no error analysis or trajectory verification is reported.

strengths: Addresses a timely and crucial bottleneck in open-ecosystem agent frameworks (MCP and the Agent Web): managing large, dynamic toolsets without prompt bloat or loss of multi-turn context.
Proposes a well-conceived pipeline combining graph-based candidate expansion (with specific mutation operators), multi-agent trajectory synthesis, and an isolated Light Routing Agent architecture.

Extensive experimental evaluation across diverse domains in MCP-Universe and MCP-Mark, demonstrating consistent performance improvements over both embedding-based retrieval and generalist LLM baselines.
Valuable analysis on robustness to noise and distractors (+LiveMCP, +Mutation), demonstrating that fine-grained discriminative training mitigates interference from semantically similar tools.
Ablation studies clearly establish the necessity of multi-turn conversational history over single-turn query matching.
weaknesses: Context window ambiguity for massive candidate sets: One of the central motivations against static injection is context saturation, yet the paper's formulation models $\pi_\theta(c \mid Q, H, C)$ where $C$ is fed into the 8B router. It is unclear how the router ingests thousands of candidate specifications at inference time without encountering the exact context saturation and latency bottlenecks it aims to resolve.

Reliance on fully simulated execution: The training trajectory synthesis is entirely environment-free (simulated by GPT-4o without grounding in real execution environments or sandboxes). This risks propagating hallucinated behaviors or non-viable state transitions into router supervision.

Evaluation scale for agent routing is relatively small: The agent routing benchmark comprises only 156 synthetically generated test cases, which limits confidence in claim of universal cross-domain generalization to the Agent Web.

Lack of latency, token cost, and top-$k$ routing analysis: In a multi-turn interaction with an external router call at every step, operational overhead (wall-clock latency, token count, and failure recovery dynamics when the router picks an incorrect tool) is not sufficiently quantified.

strengths: Relevant and timely problem formulation: Addressing tool and agent routing bottlenecks in expanding ecosystems (e.g., Model Context Protocol) by moving beyond static context injection and naive embedding retrieval is practically significant.

Well-structured data synthesis framework: Combining candidate graph construction, mutation operators (e.g., parameter redesign, workflow chaining), and random-walk trajectory simulation provides an organized pipeline for creating multi-turn supervision data with hard negatives.

Comprehensive empirical comparisons: The evaluation tests the trained router against a wide array of LLM baselines (both open-weights and proprietary models) as well as embedding-based retrievers across diverse domains in MCP-Universe and MCP-Mark.
Interesting robustness and cross-setting analysis: Evaluating the impact of noise injection (+LiveMCP, +Mutation) and candidate pool expansion provides useful insights into router resilience.
weaknesses: Unclear mechanism for handling massive candidate sets during router inference: The formulation states that the router selects $c^* = \arg\max_{c \in C} \pi_\theta(c \mid Q, H, C)$, but the paper does not explain how large candidate sets $C$ (e.g., hundreds or thousands of tools) are actually passed to the 8B model. If all candidate descriptions/schemas are placed in context, context window bloat and positional bias become severe; if candidates are scored individually or in batches, inference latency would grow linearly with $|C|$. This crucial operational detail is missing.

Lack of inference cost and efficiency profiling: The Light Routing Agent is claimed to be lightweight, but performing an 8B LLM generation/forward pass over dialogue history at every decision turn adds significant latency and computational cost compared to embedding retrieval. No metrics regarding inference latency, FLOPS, token consumption, or throughput are provided.

Evaluation circularity and synthetic benchmark limitations: The Agent Route Benchmark consists of only 156 test samples generated using the authors' own LLM-based simulation and mutation strategy. Evaluating zero-shot generalization on a benchmark constructed with the exact same generative logic as the training pipeline risks synthetic distribution bias.

Lack of execution verification during trajectory synthesis: Trajectories and tool execution outputs are generated entirely via LLM role-play simulation without environment verification or sandbox execution. Unverified synthetic tool returns often contain hallucinated states, invalid parameter schemas, and unrealistic error trajectories.

Superficial ablation studies: The ablation study (Section 4.5) only tests the inclusion versus exclusion of dialogue history. Essential components of the proposed pipeline—such as the impact of the candidate graph versus random tool pairing, the individual utility of the five mutation operators, and the effect of synthetic dataset size—are not ablated.
